papers.what_happened: A single-centre NICU report described an imaging-anchored response phenotype to sirolimus in preterm neonates with non-immune hydrops caused by vascular and lymphatic anomalies.
papers.why_it_matters: It extends the small body of evidence on mTOR inhibition for neonatal lymphatic anomalies, a population with few options and high mortality, and connects to existing tracking of sirolimus in generalized lymphatic anomaly.
papers.what_limits_confidence: No abstract or methods are indexed, so sample size, response criteria and comparator are unverifiable; a single-centre uncontrolled neonatal series cannot separate drug effect from natural history or concurrent intensive care.

papers.title: Natural History of Fetal Non-Nuchal Lymphatic Malformations: A Single Center Retrospective Study.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To document the natural history and complications of second- and third-trimester non-nuchal lymphatic malformations (LM) and identify predictors of these complications. METHODS: We conducted a single-centre retrospective review of fetuses diagnosed with LMs between January 2015 and January 2024. Lesion size was quantified using the lymphatic malformation volume ratio (LVR): LVR = 0.523 x width x length x height (cm3) / head circumference (cm). Outcomes and LVR growth trends were analyzed using Student's t-test and a linear mixed-effects model. RESULTS: Eighteen cases were included (10 cervical, 8 axillary). Uncomplicated cervical LMs grew at 0.3 cm2/week (p < 0.001). Intralesional bleeding (n = 3) was associated with LVR > 11 cm2 and significantly higher growth rates (2.6 vs. 0.3 cm2/week; p = 0.005). All cases with LVR > 5 cm2 required subsequent tracheostomy after birth. Axillary LMs grew at 0.21 cm2/week. One case with bleeding had LVR 4.4 cm2. Median LVR was significantly lower in vaginal deliveries compared with complicated births (2.0 vs. 7.3 cm2; p = 0.03). All LVR > 4 cm2 led to delivery complications. CONCLUSION: Higher LVR predicts haemorrhage and airway intervention in cervical LMs, and delivery complications in axillary LMs. These exploratory observations warrant confirmation in larger prospective cohorts.
key_findings: Eighteen fetuses with second- and third-trimester non-nuchal lymphatic malformations (10 cervical, 8 axillary) were reviewed retrospectively over 2015-2024.
Lymphatic malformation volume ratio (LVR) above 11 cm2 was associated with intralesional bleeding and faster growth (2.6 vs 0.3 cm2/week, p = 0.005).
All cases with LVR above 5 cm2 required tracheostomy after birth, and all with LVR above 4 cm2 had delivery complications.
Authors describe the observations as exploratory and requiring confirmation in larger prospective cohorts.
papers.what_happened: A single-centre retrospective review of 18 fetuses with non-nuchal lymphatic malformations reported that a larger lymphatic malformation volume ratio was associated with intralesional haemorrhage, post-natal airway intervention and delivery complications.
papers.why_it_matters: Prenatal counselling and delivery planning for congenital lymphatic malformations currently rest on very little quantitative natural-history data, and a size-based threshold would be practically useful if it replicates.
papers.what_limits_confidence: Only 18 cases at one centre with retrospectively derived thresholds and no independent validation set; the authors themselves label the findings exploratory, and multiple thresholds tested on a small sample invite overfitting.

papers.title: A single-center retrospective study of a decade-long experience in managing pediatric lymphatic malformation.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Lymphatic malformations (LMs) are rare pediatric conditions that present variable symptoms depending on lesion size and anatomical location, necessitating diverse treatment approaches. This study aims to characterize the clinical features and prognosis of LMs across different anatomical sites and to compare the therapeutic efficacy of various treatment modalities. MATERIALS AND METHODS: A retrospective analysis was performed on 478 pediatric patients diagnosed with LMs at Beijing Children's Hospital between January 2014 and December 2024. Data regarding patient demographics, clinical characteristics, treatment modalities, and therapeutic outcomes were extracted and analyzed. RESULTS: The head and neck region was the most involved site (45.0%). Macrocysts were predominantly located in the pelvic/abdominal, mixed cysts in the head and neck, and microcysts in the trunk/extremities (p < 0.01). The macrocystic subtype demonstrated the most favorable response across all therapeutic modalities (p < 0.05). Furthermore, no statistically significant difference in effective rates was observed between surgery and sclerotherapy. CONCLUSIONS: Subtype distribution demonstrated distinct anatomic predilections. Surgery and sclerotherapy both achieve high effective rates when selected according to appropriate clinical indications. Macrocystic LMs appeared to have the b
key_findings: Retrospective analysis of 478 pediatric patients with lymphatic malformations treated at a single Chinese centre between 2014 and 2024.
Head and neck was the most involved site (45.0%); macrocysts predominated in pelvic/abdominal sites, mixed cysts in head and neck, microcysts in trunk/extremities (p < 0.01).
The macrocystic subtype had the most favourable response across all treatment modalities (p < 0.05).
No statistically significant difference in effective rates was observed between surgery and sclerotherapy.
papers.what_happened: A retrospective single-centre series of 478 children with lymphatic malformations described anatomic subtype distribution and reported no significant difference in effective rates between surgery and sclerotherapy, with macrocystic lesions responding best.
papers.why_it_matters: This is one of the larger pediatric lymphatic malformation cohorts reported and supports subtype-guided rather than modality-driven treatment selection.
papers.what_limits_confidence: Treatment was not randomised, so confounding by indication is severe - lesions selected for surgery differ systematically from those selected for sclerotherapy - and 'effective rate' is a non-standardised surrogate from a single centre.

papers.title: Robot-assisted resection of abdominal lymphatic malformations in children: a novel minimally invasive strategy for complex lesions.
papers.abstract: Robotic-assisted surgery (RAS) represents a promising emerging alternative to conventional laparoscopic surgery (LAS) for abdominal lymphatic malformations (ALMs). We aimed to evaluate the safety and efficacy of robotic-assisted resection of ALMs in pediatric patients. A retrospective analysis was performed on 134 children with ALMs who underwent surgery from December 2018 to December 2025 at the Department of General Surgery, Children's Hospital, Zhejiang University School of Medicine. Patients were stratified into two groups according to the surgical modality: the robot-assisted surgery (RAS) group (n = 57) and the laparoscopic surgery (LAS) group (n = 77). The RAS group achieved a higher rate of total intracorporeal cyst dissection (33 vs. 13) and intracorporeal intestinal resection with anastomosis (21 vs. 1), whereas the LAS group more commonly used extracorporeal procedures (31 vs. 0; 32 vs. 3), with significant differences in surgical approach distribution (P < 0.001). The total hospitalization cost was significantly higher in the RAS group than in the LAS group [68286 (60183, 72551) yuan vs. 19261 (15651, 23869) yuan, P < 0.001]. Postoperatively, four complications occurred in the RAS group, while seven complications were observed in the LAS group. RAS appears to be a safe and feasible minimally invasive approach for pediatric ALMs. For complex lesions, RAS may offer ad
key_findings: Retrospective comparison of 134 children with abdominal lymphatic malformations: 57 robot-assisted versus 77 laparoscopic resections, 2018-2025.
The robotic group achieved more total intracorporeal cyst dissection (33 vs 13) and more intracorporeal intestinal resection with anastomosis (21 vs 1).
The laparoscopic group more often required extracorporeal procedures.
papers.what_happened: A retrospective single-centre comparison of robot-assisted versus laparoscopic resection of abdominal lymphatic malformations in 134 children reported more fully intracorporeal procedures in the robotic group.
papers.why_it_matters: Abdominal lymphatic malformations are technically demanding developmental lymphatic lesions, and operative approach affects morbidity in a pediatric population.
papers.what_limits_confidence: Non-randomised retrospective allocation across a period during which robotic capability was being introduced makes selection bias and temporal confounding likely, and the reported endpoints are technical process measures rather than patient outcomes.

papers.title: Expectorated bronchial casts revealing lymphatic plastic bronchitis due to thoracic duct agenesis: case report.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Plastic bronchitis is a rare disorder most often linked to aberrant lymphatic drainage or congenital and acquired cardiac anomalies. In patients with lymphatic flow abnormalities, leakage or anomalous lymphatic-bronchial communications can allow lymphatic fluid to enter the airways, where it solidifies into gelatinous or rubbery bronchial casts that may obstruct airflow and are typically expectorated. CASE PRESENTATION: A 49-year-old man presented with chronic, recurrent expectoration of pale bronchial casts accompanied by episodic dyspnea and intermittent fever. A chest CT demonstrated right-lower-lobe ground-glass opacities, interstitial changes with a lymphatic distribution pattern, and mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Bronchoscopy was unremarkable, and sputum microbiology was negative. Pulmonary function testing showed a mild obstruction. Cytologic evaluation of an expelled cast revealed mucus with fibrin, erythrocytes, macrophages, lymphocytes, and neutrophils. MR lymphangiography identified a congenital absence of the thoracic duct. Abdominal lymph drained through two markedly dilated lymphatic vessels converging in the retromediastinum and supplying predominantly right-sided pulmonary lymphatics, with a normal left-sided system. These findings established the diagnosis of lymphatic plastic bronchitis due to thoracic duct agenesis. The patient declined lymphatic i
key_findings: A 49-year-old man with recurrent expectoration of bronchial casts was found on MR lymphangiography to have congenital absence of the thoracic duct.
Abdominal lymph drained via two markedly dilated retromediastinal vessels supplying predominantly right-sided pulmonary lymphatics.
The patient declined lymphatic intervention and remains chronically symptomatic.
papers.what_happened: A case report described adult-onset lymphatic plastic bronchitis caused by congenital thoracic duct agenesis, diagnosed by MR lymphangiography after unremarkable bronchoscopy.
papers.why_it_matters: It documents a developmental central lymphatic anomaly presenting for the first time in adulthood, reinforcing that congenital lymphatic malformations can remain clinically silent for decades.
papers.what_limits_confidence: Single case report with no intervention performed and no follow-up outcome, so it carries descriptive value only and supports no management inference.

papers.title: Thoracic duct stenting as a treatment for chylothorax and chylous ascites in patient with Yellow nail syndrome.
papers.journal: Biomedical papers of the Medical Faculty of the University Palacky, Olomouc, Czechoslovakia
papers.abstract: PURPOSE: To report the approach, technical success, safety, and short-term outcomes of thoracic duct stenting for treating chylothorax and chylous ascites in a patient with Yellow Nail Syndrome. CASE REPORT: A 57-year-old male with Yellow Nail Syndrome, characterized by yellow thickened nails, lymphedema, and respiratory abnormalities, required repeated thoracocenteses for chylothorax. A thoracic duct intervention involving percutaneous transluminal angioplasty and balloon-expandable stent implantation via retrograde access was performed. Procedure characteristics, clinical success, complications, and follow-up were recorded. CONCLUSIONS: Thoracic duct stenting was a safe and technically successful procedure. After the procedure, the patient was relieved of symptoms. This technique could be considered for patients with recurrent chylothorax and chylous ascites, including those with Yellow Nail Syndrome. Further research is required to validate these findings.
key_findings: A 57-year-old man with Yellow Nail Syndrome (yellow nails, lymphedema, respiratory abnormalities) and recurrent chylothorax underwent thoracic duct angioplasty and balloon-expandable stent implantation via retrograde access.
The procedure was technically successful and the patient's symptoms resolved over short-term follow-up.
papers.what_happened: A case report described technically successful thoracic duct stenting for chylothorax and chylous ascites in one patient with Yellow Nail Syndrome, with symptom relief at short-term follow-up.
papers.why_it_matters: Yellow Nail Syndrome is a primary lymphatic dysfunction disorder with limited treatment options for refractory chylous effusions, and central lymphatic intervention is an expanding area.
papers.what_limits_confidence: A single case with short follow-up cannot establish safety or durability, and the report's conclusion that the technique 'was safe' generalises well beyond what n=1 supports.

papers.title: Clavicular Gorham-Stout disease: a rare case report and literature review.
papers.abstract: Gorham-Stout disease (GSD) is a rare idiopathic osteolytic disorder, and its diagnosis depends on a comprehensive evaluation of clinical, imaging, and pathological findings, alongside the systematic exclusion of other diseases. We report a case of GSD characterized by progressive clavicular bone destruction and resorption following low-energy trauma. Monitoring biochemical markers related to bone turnover is essential for early diagnosis and disease assessment, which is critical for controlling disease progression. The early administration of osteoclast activity inhibitors, combined with active vitamin D supplementation, can improve prognosis. Treatment plans should be individualized based on the lesion site, the patient's age, and specific needs. In clinical practice, the routine internal fixation of fractures without a definitive diagnosis may lead to severe consequences.
key_findings: Case report of Gorham-Stout disease with progressive clavicular bone destruction following low-energy trauma, plus a narrative literature review.
Authors suggest bone-turnover marker monitoring aids early diagnosis and that early osteoclast inhibition with active vitamin D may improve prognosis.
Authors caution that routine internal fixation of fractures before a definitive diagnosis may cause harm.
papers.what_happened: A single case report of clavicular Gorham-Stout disease with an accompanying literature review described the diagnostic workup and proposed early antiresorptive therapy.
papers.why_it_matters: Gorham-Stout disease is a complex lymphatic anomaly within the primary lymphatic disease spectrum, and the caution against fixing fractures before diagnosis is a practical point for surgeons.
papers.what_limits_confidence: Therapeutic claims about early osteoclast inhibition rest on one uncontrolled case plus narrative review, which cannot support prognostic benefit; the treatment recommendation is stronger than the evidence presented.

papers.title: Multifocal lymphangioma involving the liver, spleen, and retroperitoneum: A rare adult presentation.
papers.abstract: Hepatic lymphangioma is an extremely rare benign tumor of the lymphatic system, especially in adults. It often presents as a cystic lesion and can mimic other hepatic or abdominal cystic diseases such as hydatid cysts or cystadenomas. Due to its rarity and nonspecific imaging features, diagnosis is often challenging and confirmed only by histopathology. We report a 40-year-old male who presented with several months of abdominal discomfort and mild distension. Physical examination revealed no tenderness, and laboratory results were within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasound showed multiple cystic lesions throughout the liver. Further CT and MRI imaging demonstrated multiple well-defined, hypodense cystic lesions in the liver, spleen, and retroperitoneal space. The largest lesion was located adjacent to the psoas muscle and anterior to the lumbar spine, showing an insinuating appearance characteristic of lymphangioma. Surgical excision and histopathological examination confirmed the diagnosis of hepatic and retroperitoneal lymphangioma. Intrahepatic lymphangioma is a rare benign lesion that can present with multifocal abdominal involvement. Awareness of this condition is important to avoid misdiagnosis and unnecessary extensive surgery. Complete surgical excision remains the definitive treatment, providing both diagnostic confirmation and excellent prognosis.
key_findings: A 40-year-old man presented with abdominal discomfort and was found to have multifocal cystic lesions in liver, spleen and retroperitoneum.
Diagnosis of lymphangioma was confirmed only on histopathology after surgical excision, having been indistinguishable on imaging from hydatid cyst or cystadenoma.
papers.what_happened: A case report described multifocal visceral lymphangioma involving liver, spleen and retroperitoneum in a 40-year-old adult, diagnosed on histopathology after excision.
papers.why_it_matters: Visceral lymphatic malformations presenting in adulthood are rare and are easily mistaken for infectious or neoplastic cystic disease.
papers.what_limits_confidence: Single descriptive case report with no comparative or outcome data.

papers.title: Macrocystic lymphatic malformation with an unusual late presentation in a seven-year-old child: a case report and literature review.
papers.abstract: Lymphatic malformations are rare congenital lesions usually presenting at birth or early childhood, with delayed cases in school-age children being uncommon. We report a 7-year-old girl with a 9-month, painless, enlarging left neck mass without infection or trauma. Exam showed a soft, compressible mass in the posterior cervical triangle. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a multiloculated cystic lesion consistent with a macrocystic lymphatic malformation. Surgical excision confirmed lymphangioma, and the recovery was smooth. This case underlines the rare delayed presentation of a congenital lesion and the importance of including lymphatic malformations in pediatric neck mass diagnosis, regardless of age, highlighting imaging, and surgery's role in good outcomes.
key_findings: A 7-year-old girl presented with a 9-month enlarging painless left posterior cervical mass.
MRI showed a multiloculated cystic lesion; surgical excision confirmed macrocystic lymphatic malformation with uneventful recovery.
papers.what_happened: A case report described a congenital macrocystic lymphatic malformation presenting unusually late, at age seven, as a posterior cervical neck mass treated by excision.
papers.why_it_matters: It reinforces that congenital lymphatic malformations belong in the differential for pediatric neck masses at any age, not only in infancy.
papers.what_limits_confidence: Single case report with short follow-up and no comparative data.

papers.title: Unusual Vascular Anomalies in Plastic Surgery: A Case Series.
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Rare pediatric vascular tumors and malformations can be diagnostically and therapeutically challenging. They may present atypically, mimic more common conditions, or be life-threatening. Understanding of the various conditions, early recognition, and multidisciplinary management are essential for successful treatment. METHODS: A retrospective review was performed of selected pediatric vascular anomaly cases managed at a tertiary referral center between March 2023 and August 2025. Cases were chosen based on diagnostic complexity, rarity, and the requirement for multidisciplinary and/or targeted systemic therapy. CASE PRESENTATION SUMMARY: Five cases are presented: kaposiform hemangioendothelioma with Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon, congenital hemangioma, generalized lymphatic anomaly, and PIK3CA-related overgrowth spectrum disorder presenting with multifocal osteolytic lesions and fractures. Diagnoses were established through radiologic, histopathologic, and targeted genetic and molecular testing. Management combined wound care and reconstruction with systemic therapies. Propranolol was used as first-line therapy in infantile hemangioma, corticosteroids and sirolimus were used in vascular tumors with hematological complications, and alpelisib was utilized in PIK3CA-related disease. Outcomes were variable but demonstrated significant symptomatic and functional improvem

Cases included generalized lymphatic anomaly and PIK3CA-related overgrowth spectrum with multifocal osteolytic lesions and fractures.
Targeted systemic therapy was used according to molecular diagnosis: sirolimus for vascular tumours with haematological complications, alpelisib for PIK3CA-related disease.
Outcomes were described as variable but with symptomatic and functional improvement and good tolerance.
papers.what_happened: A retrospective five-case series from a tertiary centre described genotype-directed systemic therapy, including sirolimus and alpelisib, for rare pediatric vascular and lymphatic anomalies such as generalized lymphatic anomaly and PIK3CA-related overgrowth.
papers.why_it_matters: It adds to the accumulating descriptive experience with molecularly targeted therapy in developmental lymphatic anomalies, where treatment is largely off-label and evidence-poor.
papers.what_limits_confidence: Cases were explicitly selected for rarity and complexity, which precludes any estimate of response rate; there is no control group, and outcome assessment is unstandardised.

papers.title: Evaluation of patients presenting to a multidisciplinary lymphatic center.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Lymphedema is a prevalent yet underserved condition. Expanding diagnostic and therapeutic options have increased interest in multidisciplinary care. This study examines clinical characteristics and geographic patterns of lymphedema care within a multidisciplinary lymphatic center. METHODS: A retrospective review included all patients evaluated for edema at the BIDMC Lymphatic Center between January 2018 and December 2023. The multidisciplinary team was comprised of cardiovascular medicine, radiology, plastic surgery, and physical therapy. A RedCap registry captured demographics, clinical characteristics, imaging and surgeries. Patients were stratified by edema etiology as primary or secondary lymphedema, or non-lymphatic edema. Bivariate and geospatial analyses assessed differences across groups and geographic access to care. RESULTS: Of the total 2,031 participants, 76% were female, with a mean age of 60 years (±15.2) and BMI of 33.6 kg/m2 (±10.7). The average duration of edema symptoms at evaluation was 9.47 years (±11.8). Secondary lymphedema was the most common etiology (n=1,104, 54%) andoften due to cancer (54%) or chronic venous disease (23%). Lymphatic imaging was performed in 549 patients (27%). Of those 549, lymphoscintigraphy (83%) and MRI (69%) were most common. Only 149 patients (11%) underwent surgery. Residing out-of-state was associated with longer sy
key_findings: Retrospective registry review of 2,031 patients evaluated for edema at a multidisciplinary lymphatic centre, 2018-2023, stratified by primary lymphedema, secondary lymphedema, or non-lymphatic edema.
Secondary lymphedema was the most common etiology (n=1,104, 54%), leaving a substantial primary and non-lymphatic remainder.
Mean symptom duration before evaluation was 9.47 years, indicating long diagnostic delay.
Lymphatic imaging was performed in only 27% of patients and just 11% underwent surgery.
Living out-of-state was associated with longer symptom duration at presentation (12.3 vs 9.1 years) and higher surgical rates.
papers.what_happened: A retrospective registry analysis of 2,031 patients at one multidisciplinary lymphatic centre characterised edema etiology, imaging use and geography, finding a mean 9.5-year delay between symptom onset and specialist evaluation.
papers.why_it_matters: It quantifies diagnostic delay and geographic access barriers in a cohort that explicitly separates primary from secondary lymphedema, which is directly relevant to service planning and to how late primary-lymphedema patients typically reach specialist care.
papers.what_limits_confidence: Single tertiary referral centre with strong selection bias toward patients able to travel, retrospective chart-derived data, and the primary-lymphedema subgroup size and characteristics are not broken out in the abstract; the article also appeared online several months before this print issue, so it is not a new disclosure.

papers.title: Tissue Sodium Response to Complete Decongestive Therapy in Lower Extremity Lymphedema.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Lower extremity lymphedema affects a growing number of cancer survivors. Standard-of-care therapy for lymphedema is complete decongestive therapy (CDT), yet the primary outcome measurement of therapeutic efficacy is limb volume, which is relatively insensitive to both well-managed and severe disease. The primary goal of this study was to examine whether physiological sodium magnetic resonance imaging (23Na-MRI) is sensitive to the effect of CDT on leg lymphedema, and how this effect compares with the measurement reproducibility limits. METHODS AND RESULTS: Participants with lymphedema (n = 11) underwent ≥5 sessions of CDT per participant in their affected leg(s) (n = 12) over 9.2 ± 5.6 weeks, following individual treatment plans with a licensed therapist. At the baseline visit and intervention visit, at least one leg was scanned with 23Na-MRI to measure tissue sodium content (TSC) in the skin, muscle, and adipose tissue. Control subjects (n = 16) were scanned at two visits separated by a similar timeframe with no treatment to establish measurement reproducibility. Skin TSC significantly reduced by 4.32 mmol/L (p = 0.027) in affected legs treated by CDT, a change greater than the reproducibility coefficient (RPC) (3.82 mmol/L) in controls. Adipose TSC decreased in treated legs (2.27 mmol/L; p = 0.046), a change less than the RPC (5.83 mmol/L). Muscle TSC (p = 0.171)
key_findings: Eleven participants with lower extremity lymphedema (12 legs) underwent at least five sessions of complete decongestive therapy over 9.2 +/- 5.6 weeks with 23Na-MRI before and after.
Skin tissue sodium content fell by 4.32 mmol/L (p = 0.027), exceeding the 3.82 mmol/L reproducibility coefficient established in 16 untreated controls.
Adipose tissue sodium fell by 2.27 mmol/L (p = 0.046) but by less than its reproducibility coefficient.
Muscle sodium (p = 0.171) and leg circumference (p = 0.764) did not change.
papers.what_happened: An uncontrolled pre/post study in 11 participants found that skin tissue sodium measured by 23Na-MRI decreased after complete decongestive therapy by more than the measurement reproducibility limit, while leg circumference did not change.
papers.why_it_matters: If replicated, a sodium imaging readout sensitive to therapy when limb circumference is not could improve endpoint selection for lymphedema trials, where volume is known to be insensitive.
papers.what_limits_confidence: Only 11 participants in a single-arm pre/post design with no untreated lymphedema comparator (controls were used only to estimate measurement reproducibility), the endpoint is a surrogate with no linked clinical benefit, and lymphedema etiology is not specified; it directly follows an earlier report from the same group already tracked as pm_42286847.

papers.title: Secondary prevention of cellulitis: A systematic review.
papers.abstract: ObjectivesCellulitis is a common and often recurrent bacterial skin infection. Antibiotics are the first-line treatment for cellulitis and antibiotic prophylaxis is a known preventive measure for frequent recurrence. Evidence for other interventions targeting known risk factors (secondary prevention) remains unclear. This review evaluates the evidence for managing risk factors to prevent recurrent limb cellulitis.Study designA systematic review of studies on cellulitis risk factor management, excluding antibiotic prophylaxis, was conducted. Five databases were searched in February 2023 and June 2024. Eligible studies underwent narrative synthesis and quality assessment. Databases searched included MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, CINAHL, and EMBASE, for the time period 1996-June 2024.Data synthesisSummary of major results; Of 1,116 screened papers, 25 met the criteria. Study designs varied, with only one randomized controlled trial. Nearly all studies addressed lymphoedema, showing that its management, particularly with compression, consistently reduced cellulitis recurrence. Although cellulitis guidelines detail the need to address many risk factors to reduce cellulitis, including tinea and ulcers, we did not find studies that linked the management of these conditions with cellulitis recurrence.ConclusionsEvidence strongly supports lymphoedema management in preventing cellulit
key_findings: Systematic review of interventions for recurrent limb cellulitis that target risk factors other than antibiotic prophylaxis; five databases searched to June 2024.
Of 1,116 papers screened, 25 met criteria, and nearly all addressed lymphoedema as the dominant modifiable risk factor.
Only one of the 25 included studies was a randomised controlled trial; the remainder required narrative synthesis.
papers.what_happened: A systematic review of non-antibiotic secondary prevention of recurrent limb cellulitis identified 25 eligible studies, nearly all centred on lymphoedema management, of which only one was a randomised trial.
papers.why_it_matters: Recurrent cellulitis is one of the few genuinely patient-important endpoints in primary lymphedema and a major driver of morbidity and progression, so the strength of evidence behind lymphoedema-directed prevention matters directly to counselling.
papers.what_limits_confidence: The included evidence is almost entirely non-randomised and heterogeneous enough to preclude meta-analysis, the search closed in June 2024 so the synthesis is already dated, and 'secondary prevention' here denotes preventing recurrence rather than secondary lymphedema.

papers.title: Management and prevention of lower leg cellulitis: a survey assessing practice variation and equipoise among Australasian clinicians in preparation for a randomised clinical trial.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Lower limb cellulitis accounts for 1.5%-2% of visits to Australasian emergency departments. Antibiotics are considered the cornerstone of management, but despite prioritisation by consumers, acute interventions to manage pain and inflammation and cellulitis recurrence prevention strategies remain understudied beyond small pilot trials. AIMS: We aimed to assess clinicians' current practices, areas of clinical uncertainty and willingness to randomise patients to interventions, including demarcation lines, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), corticosteroids, compression therapy, exercise, antibiotic prophylaxis and a hypothetical streptococcal vaccine for cellulitis prevention. METHODS: A cross-sectional online survey, consisting of 22 questions assessing clinical practices and equipoise for randomisation into a future trial, was distributed to practicing Australasian clinicians specialising in infectious diseases, lymphoedema physiotherapy, internal medicine, emergency medicine or surgery. RESULTS: A total of 250 (response rate of ~10%) respondents completed the survey from 77 unique institutions. Lower limb cellulitis was common, with 91 respondents reporting >200 presentations at their institution annually. For most assessment, management and prevention strategies, there was wide variation in clinical practice. Overall, respondents were comfortable consi
key_findings: Cross-sectional survey of 250 Australasian clinicians (approximately 10% response rate) across infectious diseases, lymphoedema physiotherapy, internal medicine, emergency medicine and surgery.
Wide practice variation was reported across nearly all assessment, management and prevention strategies for lower limb cellulitis.
Respondents expressed willingness to randomise patients to interventions including demarcation lines, NSAIDs, corticosteroids, compression therapy, exercise and antibiotic prophylaxis.
papers.what_happened: A survey of 250 Australasian clinicians documented wide practice variation in lower limb cellulitis management and confirmed equipoise for randomising several prevention interventions, in preparation for a future randomised trial.
papers.why_it_matters: It signals a forthcoming randomised trial in cellulitis prevention, an endpoint that matters more to primary lymphedema patients than limb volume, and is worth adding to the watchlist.
papers.what_limits_confidence: A survey with roughly 10% response rate is highly vulnerable to non-response bias and measures stated intent rather than behaviour or outcomes; no trial has yet been registered or reported in this record.

papers.title: A systematic review of contemporary randomized controlled trials for treatment of lower extremity lymphedema by intermittent pneumatic compression devices.
papers.journal: Journal of vascular surgery. Venous and lymphatic disorders
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Observational trials have suggested that intermittent pneumatic compression (IPC) devices reduce lymphedema (LED) volume and improve patient-reported outcomes, but this type of trial is subject to bias. Systematic reviews (SRs) of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) provide the highest evidentiary strength for examining the impact of a therapeutic intervention and are important for evidence-based clinical practice guidelines. Few existing SRs, however, include recent RCTs and only a smaller number address LED of the lower extremities (LELED). Therefore, we conducted a SR based on PICO questions to identify RCTs that examined the effect of IPC on LELED for a clinical practice guideline. METHODS: For this SR, English-language RCTs in CINAHL, Embase, and MEDLINE published between January 1, 2010, and January 31, 2025, were searched and the PRISMA reporting method was used. Both intragroup and intergroup comparisons of the specified outcome measures were examined for statistical significance. The evidentiary quality of the RCTs and risk of bias were assessed using GRADE and the Cochrane risk of bias tool, respectively. RESULTS: In the PRISMA analysis, 141 articles were identified through a search of the databases and an additional 4 articles were discovered through other sources, for a total of 145 eligible RCTs. Twenty-one RCTs addressed upper extremity LED and seven LE
key_findings: Systematic review restricted to randomised controlled trials of intermittent pneumatic compression for lower extremity lymphedema, published January 2010 to January 2025, conducted to inform a clinical practice guideline.
Of 145 eligible RCTs identified, 21 addressed upper extremity lymphedema and only seven met inclusion criteria for lower extremity disease.
Evidentiary quality was assessed with GRADE and risk of bias with the Cochrane tool.
The small number of lower-extremity RCTs relative to upper-extremity ones documents a persistent asymmetry in the evidence base.
papers.what_happened: A GRADE-assessed systematic review of randomised trials found only seven RCTs of intermittent pneumatic compression for lower extremity lymphedema published between 2010 and 2025, compared with 21 for upper extremity disease.
papers.why_it_matters: This is the methodologically strongest synthesis in this scan window and it feeds directly into a clinical practice guideline; lower extremity disease is where most primary lymphedema presents, so the thin RCT base is a scope-relevant evidence gap.
papers.what_limits_confidence: Only seven small RCTs were available, outcomes are predominantly volume-based surrogates rather than cellulitis or function, the search closed in January 2025, and the constituent trials' etiology mix (primary versus secondary) is not specified in the abstract.

papers.title: A systematic review of selection criteria for extirpative and combined surgical procedures in lower extremity lymphedema.
papers.journal: Journal of vascular surgery. Venous and lymphatic disorders
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Advanced lower extremity lymphedema is difficult to manage and can lead to significant functional impairment and diminished quality of life. Extirpative (also known as excisional and debulking) surgical procedures offer meaningful volume reduction for patients with advanced disease refractory to conservative management. The objective of this systematic review was to identify the clinical and imaging criteria used to determine candidacy for excisional surgery (ie, Charles and modified Homan procedures) in adults with lower extremity lymphedema and to report the surgical outcomes observed across the included studies. METHODS: A systematic search of PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Library was conducted by an expert medical librarian. The search yielded 3916 articles. Inclusion criteria involved randomized controlled trials, cohort studies, and case series that reported on excisional surgical procedures for adults with lower extremity lymphedema and described clinical or imaging criteria for surgical candidacy. Studies that did not involve patients with lower extremity lymphedema were excluded. Screening, full-text review, and data extraction were performed using Covidence software (Veritas Health Innovation) with standardized data extraction templates. This review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guide
key_findings: Systematic review of clinical and imaging criteria used to select adults with lower extremity lymphedema for excisional (debulking) surgery.
From 3,916 screened articles, only five studies totalling 933 patients met inclusion criteria.
Extirpative procedures are positioned for advanced disease refractory to conservative management.
papers.what_happened: A systematic review found only five studies (933 patients) reporting explicit clinical or imaging criteria for selecting lower extremity lymphedema patients for excisional debulking surgery.
papers.why_it_matters: Advanced primary lower extremity lymphedema is a population in which debulking is still used, and the near-absence of documented selection criteria is a concrete evidence gap for surgical decision-making.
papers.what_limits_confidence: Only five heterogeneous non-randomised studies were available, none randomised, and the review reflects the same single-arm retrospective evidence base that characterises lymphedema surgery generally; primary versus secondary etiology is not separated.

papers.title: A systematic review on clinical and imaging criteria for liposuction candidacy in lower extremity lymphedema.
papers.journal: Journal of vascular surgery. Venous and lymphatic disorders
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Lower-extremity lymphedema is difficult to treat, especially after failing conservative management. Liposuction (also termed lipoaspiration or suction-assisted lipectomy) has been identified as a treatment option for patients who failed conservative management in lower-extremity lymphedema. This systematic review evaluates the clinical and imaging criteria used to determine candidacy for liposuction in adults with lower-extremity lymphedema. METHODS: A systematic review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines. The review searched Embase, PubMed, and Cochrane Library from inception through April 2026. Six reviewers screened 3057 studies using Covidence software. Of the 74 full-text articles assessed, seven studies met inclusion criteria. Inclusion criteria were cohort studies with greater than 50 participants and systematic reviews containing extractable lower-extremity liposuction data in patients with lymphedema. Studies were excluded for wrong study design, wrong surgical procedure, or absence of extractable lower-extremity data. Outcomes of interest were limb volume reduction, cellulitis frequency, quality of life, functional status, and compression garment dependency. Evidence was synthesized narratively due to heterogeneity across studies. RESULTS: Seven studies were included: 3 prospect
key_findings: Systematic review of criteria for liposuction candidacy in adults with lower extremity lymphedema, searched to April 2026.
Seven studies met criteria: three prospective cohorts (n=190), two retrospective cohorts (n=145), and two systematic reviews.
Outcomes of interest included limb volume reduction, cellulitis frequency, quality of life, functional status and compression garment dependency.
Heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis; evidence was synthesised narratively.
papers.what_happened: A systematic review identified seven studies addressing clinical and imaging criteria for liposuction candidacy in lower extremity lymphedema, with heterogeneity too great for meta-analysis.
papers.why_it_matters: Liposuction is increasingly offered for fibrofatty-stage lymphedema including primary disease, and this review makes explicit how little standardised selection guidance exists.
papers.what_limits_confidence: No randomised evidence, small cohorts, narrative synthesis only, and the review does not separate primary from secondary lymphedema populations; volume remains the dominant reported endpoint.

papers.title: Vascularized Lymphatic Tissue Transfer for Treatment of Lower Limb Lymphedema: Does the Recipient Site Matter?
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Vascularized lymph node transfer (VLNT) is a pivotal component in lower limb lymphedema (LLL) treatment. We aimed to assess the association of using the groin and ankle as single or multilevel recipient sites on both limb volume reduction and recipient site morbidity. METHODS: A total of 51 patients with LLL received VLNT between 2016 and 2023. We assessed volume preoperatively and postoperatively over a 12-mo period. We compared limb volume changes in primary lymphedema (PLE) and secondary lymphedema (SLE) subgroups depending on recipient sites: groin, ankle, and multilevel (groin and ankle). Recipient site complications were noted. RESULTS: Multilevel inset showed a higher volume reduction than the single level proximally (P = 0.002) or distally (P = 0.002) predominantly in PLE. No difference was found between distal and proximal recipient sites alone. In SLE, we did not observe a higher volume reduction with a multilevel approach. Multilevel inset showed a lower ratio of major recipient site complications. CONCLUSIONS: Limb volume reduction in VLNT varies depending on the recipient site. In PLE, a multilevel approach showed higher volume reduction without an increase in complication rates and might thus be favored. Single-level proximal and multilevel insets showed similar outcomes in our small SLE cohort, indicating that a single-level approach may be adequate
key_findings: Retrospective series of 51 patients undergoing vascularized lymph node transfer for lower limb lymphedema, 2016-2023, with 12-month volume follow-up.
Multilevel (groin plus ankle) inset showed greater volume reduction than either single proximal (p = 0.002) or single distal (p = 0.002) recipient site.
The multilevel advantage was reported as predominant in the primary lymphedema subgroup; no such difference was observed in the secondary lymphedema subgroup.
No difference was found between distal and proximal recipient sites used alone.
papers.what_happened: A retrospective 51-patient series reported that multilevel groin-plus-ankle recipient siting for vascularized lymph node transfer produced greater 12-month limb volume reduction than single-site inset, with the effect described as concentrated in the primary lymphedema subgroup.
papers.why_it_matters: Surgical series reporting primary lymphedema outcomes separately from secondary disease are uncommon, and recipient-site strategy is a modifiable technical decision.
papers.what_limits_confidence: This is a retrospective, non-randomised comparison of 51 patients with an unspecified primary-subgroup size, volume as the sole endpoint over only 12 months, no adjustment for weight or BMI change, and a subgroup interaction that is exploratory rather than pre-specified.

papers.title: Superb Microvascular Imaging-Enhanced Lymphatic Ultrasound for Preoperative Mapping in Lymphedema-related Lymphaticovenular Anastomosis.
papers.journal: Plastic and reconstructive surgery. Global open
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Accurate preoperative identification of functional lymphatic vessels and veins is essential for successful lymphaticovenular anastomosis (LVA). Conventional Doppler-based ultrasonography (D-CUPS [Doppler, cross, uncollapsible, parallel, superficial fascia]) may produce motion-related artifacts that complicate lymphatic-venous discrimination. This study compares examination time and examiner burden between a superb microvascular imaging-based method (S-CUPS) and D-CUPS for preoperative LVA mapping. METHODS: Twenty patients with primary or secondary lymphedema underwent both D-CUPS and S-CUPS in randomized order before LVA. In 36 limbs, 88 predefined scanning sites were evaluated. Per-site examination time, vessel depth and diameter, intraoperative NECST classification (normal, ectasis, contraction, sclerosis), and examiner fatigue using a 1-10 visual analog scale (VAS) were recorded. Linear mixed-effects models accounted for clustering of multiple sites within patients, and Spearman correlation analyses were performed for continuous variables. All ultrasound-identified veins and lymphatic vessels were confirmed intraoperatively. RESULTS: S-CUPS shortened per-site examination time compared with D-CUPS (estimated marginal means, 51.7 versus 75.0 s; P = 0.0193). Mental VAS scores were lower with S-CUPS (1.24 ± 0.64 versus 1.86 ± 0.69; P < 0.001), whereas physical VAS sc
key_findings: Twenty patients with primary or secondary lymphedema underwent both superb-microvascular-imaging (S-CUPS) and Doppler-based (D-CUPS) preoperative mapping in randomised order across 36 limbs and 88 predefined sites.
S-CUPS shortened per-site examination time (51.7 vs 75.0 seconds, p = 0.0193) and reduced examiner mental fatigue scores (1.24 vs 1.86, p < 0.001).
Physical fatigue scores did not differ significantly (p = 0.19).
All ultrasound-identified vessels were confirmed intraoperatively, providing a reference standard.
papers.what_happened: A within-patient randomised-order comparison in 20 lymphedema patients found that superb microvascular imaging shortened preoperative lymphatic mapping time and reduced examiner mental fatigue relative to Doppler-based mapping, with intraoperative confirmation of identified vessels.
papers.why_it_matters: Randomised-order within-patient design with an intraoperative reference standard is unusually rigorous for a lymphedema imaging technique study, and the cohort explicitly includes primary lymphedema.
papers.what_limits_confidence: Only 20 patients at a single centre, examiners could not be blinded to imaging modality, and the endpoints are workflow measures (examination time, operator fatigue) rather than surgical or patient outcomes.

papers.title: Lymphatic Ultrasound in Longitudinal Decision-making for Lymphedema: A Narrative Review Integrating Conservative and Surgical Management.
papers.journal: Plastic and reconstructive surgery. Global open
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Lymphedema is a chronic and progressive condition that requires long-term reassessment and adaptation of treatment strategies. Although conservative therapy and surgical interventions such as lymphaticovenular anastomosis have advanced, imaging findings are not consistently integrated into longitudinal treatment decision-making, including treatment selection, timing, and target prioritization. METHODS: This narrative review synthesizes current evidence and practice-related concepts regarding lymphatic ultrasound. Topics include lymphatic vessel characterization, differentiation from veins, subcutaneous tissue evaluation, and elastography. Particular emphasis is placed on how these findings may inform conservative management, surgical planning, and serial reassessment during the disease course. RESULTS: Lymphatic ultrasound enables repeated, noninvasive evaluation of both lymphatic vessels and surrounding subcutaneous tissues within the same examination. When interpreted using structured approaches such as NECST (normal, ectasis, contraction, and sclerosis)-aligned vessel assessment and D-CUPS, serial ultrasound may help clinicians adjust compression strategies, identify potential windows for lymphaticovenular anastomosis, reassess treatment targets beyond the affected limb segment, and support multidisciplinary communication during follow-up. The principal conceptua
key_findings: Narrative review proposing integration of lymphatic ultrasound into longitudinal lymphedema decision-making rather than one-off surgical planning.
Synthesises vessel-based (NECST: normal, ectasis, contraction, sclerosis) and tissue-based assessment into a combined framework.
Suggests serial ultrasound may inform compression adjustment, LVA timing windows and reassessment of treatment targets.
papers.what_happened: A narrative review proposed a framework integrating vessel-level and tissue-level lymphatic ultrasound findings into longitudinal treatment decisions across conservative and surgical management.
papers.why_it_matters: Serial non-invasive imaging could in principle help time interventions in a chronic progressive disease, and ultrasound is far more accessible than lymphoscintigraphy or MR lymphangiography.
papers.what_limits_confidence: This is a conceptual narrative review with no systematic search, no validation cohort and no outcome data showing that ultrasound-guided decisions improve results.

papers.title: High-frequency ultrasound combined with microbubbles for preoperative lymphatic mapping for lymphedema with a non-linear pattern in indocyanine green lymphography.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Lymphatic-venous anastomosis (LVA) is an effective surgical treatment for lymphedema, which requires accurate identification of lymphatic vessels. Indocyanine Green (ICG) lymphography, the most common method for lymphatic mapping, cannot always successfully identify lymphatic vessels. We aimed to explore high-frequency ultrasound (HFUS) and contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) as a reliable alternative for lymphatic mapping when ICG lymphography is not feasible. MATERIALS AND METHODS: We performed combined HFUS and CEUS for lymphatic mapping on the patients who exhibited no obvious linear pattern on ICG lymphography. The inner and outer diameters and depths of the lymphatic vessels were measured. We subsequently evaluated the accuracy of US lymphatic mapping by comparing it with the operative results. And the postoperative volume and circumference of the affected limbs were compared with the preoperative measurements. RESULTS: We recruited 111 patients with lymphedema, including 96 limbs and 24 perineal areas affected. Three hundred forty-five lymphatics in the limbs and 52 in the perineum underwent anastomosis and were analyzed. Comparable lymphatic vessel diameter (inner: 0.5-0.9 mm; outer: 0.8-0.9 mm) and depth (9-10 mm) measurements across HFUS, CEUS, and combined HFUS + CEUS. However, HFUS + CEUS significantly improved detection sensitivity, identifying 313 vess
key_findings: 111 patients with lymphedema who showed no clear linear pattern on ICG lymphography underwent high-frequency and contrast-enhanced ultrasound mapping.
345 limb lymphatics and 52 perineal lymphatics were anastomosed and analysed against operative findings.
Combined HFUS plus CEUS identified 313 vessels at 91.1% accuracy versus 114 (88.6%) for HFUS alone and 22 (90.9%) for CEUS alone, improving detection sensitivity.
papers.what_happened: A prospective study in 111 lymphedema patients with non-diagnostic ICG lymphography found that combining high-frequency and contrast-enhanced ultrasound improved lymphatic vessel detection sensitivity for surgical mapping, verified against operative findings.
papers.why_it_matters: ICG lymphography fails in advanced disease where dermal backflow obscures linear vessels, and this is precisely the population, including advanced primary lymphedema, in which surgical planning is hardest.
papers.what_limits_confidence: Single-centre, non-randomised, with no blinding of ultrasound operators to prior imaging; lymphedema etiology is not specified and the perineal involvement suggests a substantial pelvic-cancer component, and the endpoints are vessel detection and volume rather than function or cellulitis.

papers.title: Finite Element Modeling of Lower Limb Lymphedema: Influence of Limb Morphology and Compression Garment Classes on Internal Pressure Distribution.
papers.abstract: PURPOSE: Compression therapy with medical graduated compression garments is commonly used in the treatment of leg lymphedema. However, the relationship between the interface pressure applied by the garment and the resulting hydrostatic pressure within the soft tissues remains poorly understood. Women commonly use thigh-high garments, whereas men often use knee-high compression garments, but the effects of these different garment types remain unclear. The objective of this study was to evaluate pressure transmission within lymphedematous legs and to assess the effects of different garment types. METHODS: Patient-specific finite element models were developed from magnetic resonance imaging data of eight female and three male lymphedematous legs. The models explicitly represented the skin, fascia cruris, subcutaneous tissue, and muscle. Interface and hydrostatic pressures were quantified for class 2 and class 3 compression garments, as well as for three garment superimposition configurations. RESULTS: For all legs wearing class 2 compression garments, and for female legs wearing class 3 compression garments, interface and hydrostatic pressures were below therapeutic ranges. Male legs wearing class 3 compression garments achieved hydrostatic pressure values within the therapeutic range due to higher garment stiffness. Superimposition of garments increased hydrostatic pressure in fe
key_findings: Patient-specific finite element models were built from MRI of 11 lymphedematous legs (8 female, 3 male), representing skin, fascia cruris, subcutaneous tissue and muscle.
For all legs in class 2 garments, and for female legs in class 3 garments, interface and hydrostatic pressures fell below therapeutic ranges.
Male legs in class 3 garments reached therapeutic hydrostatic pressure, attributed to higher garment stiffness.
Garment superimposition raised hydrostatic pressure in female legs but produced excessive compression in male legs.
papers.what_happened: A computational finite element modelling study of 11 patient-specific lymphedematous legs predicted that standard class 2 and class 3 compression garments may deliver sub-therapeutic internal tissue pressure in female limbs, while garment superimposition may over-compress male limbs.
papers.why_it_matters: Compression is the backbone of conservative management in primary lymphedema and garment class is prescribed largely by convention, so a morphology- and sex-dependent mismatch between interface pressure and internal tissue pressure would be practically relevant if validated.
papers.what_limits_confidence: These are simulated pressures from 11 models with only three male limbs, not measured tissue pressures, and no clinical outcomes were assessed; model assumptions about tissue material properties are not independently validated in vivo.

papers.title: Prevalence and Clinical Characteristics of Chronic Venous Insufficiency among Individuals with Lower Extremity Lymphoedema: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
papers.journal: European journal of vascular and endovascular surgery : the official journal of the European Society for Vascular Surgery
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Lower extremity lymphoedema is increasingly recognised as a multifactorial condition in which chronic venous insufficiency (CVI) may play an important role. This study aimed to estimate the pooled prevalence of CVI among individuals with lower extremity lymphoedema and to summarise clinical characteristics of patients with combined disease. DATA SOURCES: PubMed, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library were searched from database inception through 13 November 2025. REVIEW METHODS: Observational studies reporting CVI among individuals with lower extremity lymphoedema were included. Study selection, data extraction, and risk of bias assessments were performed independently by two reviewers. Pooled prevalence was estimated using a random effects generalised linear mixed model. RESULTS: Eighteen studies were included; 12 contributed to the prevalence meta-analysis, comprising 1 563 individuals with lower extremity lymphoedema, of whom 570 had coexisting CVI. The pooled prevalence was 45.7% (95% confidence interval [CI] 31.0 - 61.2%; GRADE, very low certainty evidence), with substantial heterogeneity (I2 = 95.6%). In a restricted analysis limited to five studies with clearer case definitions, systematic venous assessment, and well defined denominators, pooled prevalence was 48.8% (95% CI 23.1 - 75.1%; very low certainty evidence), with persistent heterogeneity (I2 = 92.2%
key_findings: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 18 studies; 12 contributed prevalence data covering 1,563 individuals with lower extremity lymphoedema.
Pooled prevalence of coexisting chronic venous insufficiency was 45.7% (95% CI 31.0-61.2%), rising to 48.8% in a restricted higher-quality analysis.
Heterogeneity was extreme (I2 = 95.6%) and GRADE certainty was rated very low.
Diagnostic criteria and clinical characteristics were inconsistently reported and most studies had moderate to high risk of bias.
Authors recommend routine venous evaluation in patients with lower extremity lymphoedema.
papers.what_happened: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 18 studies estimated that roughly half of individuals with lower extremity lymphoedema have coexisting chronic venous insufficiency, but rated the certainty of that estimate as very low.
papers.why_it_matters: Coexisting venous disease alters both diagnosis and management of lower extremity swelling, and undetected venous insufficiency is a plausible confounder in primary lymphedema outcome studies.
papers.what_limits_confidence: Heterogeneity was extreme (I2 above 95%), GRADE certainty was very low, diagnostic criteria for both conditions varied widely across studies, and the included populations do not separate primary from secondary lymphoedema; the authors are appropriately explicit about all of this.

papers.title: Local lymphatic circulation disorder: A key promoter of tissue inflammation and organ fibrosis.
papers.abstract: The lymphatic system serves as a vital vascular network essential for maintaining fluid homeostasis, macromolecule and lipid transport, and modulating immune responses. While traditional research has predominantly focused on peripheral lymphedema and secondary fibrosis resulting from local lymphatic circulation disorders, accumulating evidence indicates that lymphatic dysfunction is a key driver of systemic inflammation and fibrotic remodeling across various solid organs. This review systematically elucidates the pathological basis of peripheral lymphatic circulation disorders, including lymphatic endothelial cell dysfunction, impaired vessel contractility, lymphatic muscle cell and valve abnormalities, and abnormal permeability. Furthermore, we synthesize the core mechanism linking lymphatic failure to tissue fibrosis, specifically highlighting the crosstalk between chronic immune activation, cytokine signaling, fibroblast activation, extracellular matrix deposition, and altered lymphangiogenesis. By mapping these universal pathogenic pathways onto organ-specific diseases, spanning cardiovascular, renal, pulmonary, and hepatic systems, as well as metabolic and tumor-associated microenvironments, we demonstrate how localized lymphatic deficits precipitate broader fibrotic consequences through shared mechanisms and organ-specific amplifying pathways. Finally, we highlight the in
key_findings: Narrative review linking local lymphatic circulation disorders to tissue inflammation and fibrosis across cardiovascular, renal, pulmonary and hepatic systems.
Covers lymphatic endothelial cell dysfunction, impaired vessel contractility, lymphatic muscle cell and valve abnormalities, and abnormal permeability.
Argues for therapies that restore lymphatic integrity and drainage to interrupt progressive fibrosis.
papers.what_happened: A narrative review synthesised mechanisms by which local lymphatic circulation disorders, including valve and lymphatic muscle cell abnormalities, may drive inflammation and fibrosis in multiple organ systems.
papers.why_it_matters: Valve and contractility defects are the same mechanisms implicated in several primary lymphedema genotypes, so a cross-organ mechanistic framing may suggest shared therapeutic targets.
papers.what_limits_confidence: Narrative review with no systematic search or quality appraisal, drawing largely on preclinical work, and it does not address primary lymphedema genotypes specifically.

papers.title: Dysfunctional adipose tissue-lymphatic crosstalk in obesity.
papers.abstract: The lymphatic vasculature is recognized for its roles in immunity, lipid transport and fluid homeostasis, but has been ignored, until recently, for its involvement in adipose tissue metabolism, obesity and associated comorbidities. States of overnutrition, such as in obesity, are associated with impairment of lymphatic function, leading to localized lymphoedema, adipogenesis and insulin resistance. Conversely, compromised lymphatic vasculature integrity can induce adiposity and accelerate insulin resistance. Through the use of advanced 'omics' and bioinformatic technologies coupled with functional experiments in cells, mice and humans, we now know that the lymphatic system is more than just a transport conduit and is intimately involved in tissue and organ homeostasis, including in adipose tissue. In this Review, we summarize the interconnected causes of obesity and lymphatic dysfunction with a particular focus on delineating the underappreciated yet fundamental crosstalk between the lymphatic network and white and brown adipose tissues. We also synthesize information on lymph-directed therapeutic strategies that have the potential to transform outcomes in obesity.
key_findings: Review of bidirectional crosstalk between the lymphatic vasculature and white and brown adipose tissue.
Describes how obesity impairs lymphatic function leading to localised lymphoedema, adipogenesis and insulin resistance.
Notes the converse direction: compromised lymphatic integrity can itself induce adiposity and accelerate insulin resistance.
Summarises lymph-directed therapeutic strategies under investigation for obesity.
papers.what_happened: A review in a high-profile endocrinology journal synthesised evidence that lymphatic dysfunction and adipose tissue biology interact bidirectionally, with lymphatic impairment capable of driving adiposity and insulin resistance rather than only resulting from obesity.
papers.why_it_matters: Fibroadipose deposition is a defining feature of established primary lymphedema, and a causal arrow running from lymphatic failure to adipogenesis would reframe obesity in lymphedema as partly consequence rather than only confounder.
papers.what_limits_confidence: Narrative review without systematic methodology, built substantially on murine data, and it addresses obesity-associated lymphatic dysfunction rather than genetic primary lymphedema; journal prestige should not raise confidence in the underlying evidence.

papers.title: Congenital Distichiasis in a Young Male: A Rare Case without Systemic Association.
papers.abstract: Congenital distichiasis is a rare eyelid disorder typically associated with lymphedema-distichiasis syndrome. However, isolated forms without systemic manifestations have also been recognized. This report presents a 28-year-old male with long-standing bilateral eye rubbing and recent unilateral visual blurring. Slit-lamp examination revealed distichiasis arising from meibomian gland orifices, more prominent in the left eye, without corneal involvement. A diagnosis of isolated congenital distichiasis was made. The patient underwent selective electroepilation with complete symptom relief and no recurrence at 3 months. This case underscores the phenotypic variability of congenital distichiasis and highlights the effectiveness of electroepilation as a safe, noninvasive first-line intervention in isolated cases.
key_findings: A 28-year-old man with bilateral distichiasis arising from meibomian gland orifices was diagnosed with isolated congenital distichiasis and treated with selective electroepilation, symptom-free at 3 months.
The report notes distichiasis is typically associated with lymphedema-distichiasis syndrome but that isolated forms are recognised.
No FOXC2 genetic testing is reported in the abstract.
papers.what_happened: A case report described a 28-year-old man with congenital distichiasis reported as isolated and without systemic association, treated successfully with electroepilation at 3-month follow-up.
papers.why_it_matters: Distichiasis is the presenting and often earliest sign of lymphedema-distichiasis syndrome, so how confidently an 'isolated' label is assigned bears directly on whether FOXC2 testing and lymphedema surveillance are offered.
papers.what_limits_confidence: No FOXC2 genetic testing is reported and lymphedema in lymphedema-distichiasis syndrome commonly onsets around or after puberty with incomplete penetrance, so a clinical diagnosis of isolated distichiasis at 28 without genetic confirmation cannot exclude the syndrome; follow-up was only 3 months.

papers.title: Watershed of Collecting Lymphatic Vessels of The Hip; Between Back and Thigh.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Gluteal lymphedema is often developed by proximal edematous type of lower extremity lymphedema (LEL) and severe LEL. This study aimed to clarify the watershed of collecting lymph vessels in the gluteal region using indocyanine green (ICG) lymphography. METHODS: Medical records of cancer survivors who underwent ICG lymphography for secondary lower lymphedema screening from November 2020 to September 2023 were reviewed. Non-lymphedematous limbs without a dermal backflow pattern on ICG lymphography (ICG stage 0) were included. 0.1 mL of ICG was injected intradermally at five points; the tip of the coccygeal bone, the gluteal fold, the crosspoint connecting those points and the mid-lateral thigh, and the midpoints of them in a prone position and named H1-H5 from medial to lateral. Based on ICG lymphography findings, the posteromedial and posterolateral pathway directions of collecting lymph vessels, shown as linear patterns, from each point were investigated. RESULTS: A total of 20 limbs of 15 cancer survivors were included. The posterolateral pattern lymphatic pathway from H1/H2/H3/H4 was observed in 16/15/3/4 limbs. The posteromedial pattern lymphatic pathway from H2/H3/H4/H5 was observed in 13/15/18/10 limbs. Anteromedial pattern lymphatic pathway from H5 was observed in 6 limbs. CONCLUSIONS: Multiple ICG injections enhanced the watershed line of collecting lymphatic
key_findings: ICG lymphography with five standardised injection points mapped collecting lymphatic pathways in the gluteal region.
Twenty limbs from 15 cancer survivors were studied, but only non-lymphedematous limbs without dermal backflow (ICG stage 0) were included, so the mapping describes normal anatomy.
Posterolateral and posteromedial drainage pathways were characterised per injection point, defining a gluteal watershed line.
papers.what_happened: An ICG lymphography study of 20 non-lymphedematous limbs defined the watershed of collecting lymphatic vessels in the gluteal region.
papers.why_it_matters: Gluteal and proximal involvement occurs in advanced lower extremity lymphedema of any cause, and normal drainage anatomy underpins both diagnosis and surgical planning.
papers.what_limits_confidence: Only 20 limbs from 15 participants, all recruited as cancer survivors undergoing secondary-lymphedema screening, and the study describes normal anatomy rather than lymphedematous pathways, so extension to primary lymphedema is inferential.

papers.title: "Debulking" the future of lymphedema surgery: A narrative review.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To summarize and contextualize current and future perspectives in the surgical treatment of lymphedema, exploring new techniques and technologies, integrated treatment modalities, and their real-time clinical applications. BACKGROUND: Lymphedema is a debilitating condition caused by impaired lymphatic flow. It diminishes quality of life (QoL) and often leads to other sequential comorbidities. There is no established cure, and the optimal treatment option remains debated. Understanding current and future surgical approaches, especially the preventive and curative role at early stages, would be valuable. METHODS: A literature review was conducted using PubMed, Cochrane, and Google Scholar, including only high-impact systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and randomized controlled trials from the past 10 years. RESULTS: Lymphovenous anastomosis, vascularized lymph node transfer, and liposuction were among the most discussed surgical treatment options. Benefits include speedy volume reduction, greater QoL, and better wound healing. Microsurgical techniques greatly aided early-stage lymphedema. Fibrotic, irreversible lymphedema cases were better treated with reductive procedures and improved QoL. On the flip side, we are encountering limitations in standardization, resources, and the need for adjunctive conservative therapy while trying to make surgical treatment the mainstay
key_findings: Narrative review of current and emerging surgical treatment for lymphedema, covering lymphovenous anastomosis, vascularized lymph node transfer and liposuction.
Notes persistent limitations in standardisation and resources and continued need for adjunctive conservative therapy.
Discusses imaging, robotics and regenerative medicine as future directions.
papers.what_happened: A narrative review summarised current and emerging surgical options for lymphedema and argued for an expanded, earlier surgical role.
papers.why_it_matters: Surgical management is expanding in practice ahead of randomised evidence, so how the surgical literature frames its own certainty is worth tracking.
papers.what_limits_confidence: Despite claiming to include only high-impact systematic reviews, meta-analyses and RCTs, no systematic search method is reported; the framing of surgery as a prospective mainstay runs ahead of an evidence base that still contains essentially no randomised trials, and the article appeared online in January 2026 so this print issue is not a new disclosure.

papers.title: Vascular Anomalies: A Comprehensive Review of Etiology, Complications, and Management Strategies.
papers.abstract: Vascular anomalies encompass a group of disorders involving abnormalities of blood and lymphatic vessels, ranging from benign cutaneous lesions to complex, life-threatening conditions. These anomalies are broadly classified into vascular tumors and malformations based on underlying pathophysiology. Despite their clinical prevalence, the management of vascular anomalies remains challenging due to their diverse presentations, variable progression, and potential for significant functional and aesthetic morbidity. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the etiology, clinical presentation, complications, and management strategies of vascular anomalies, with a focus on their relevance to plastic and reconstructive surgery. Vascular tumors, including infantile hemangiomas, congenital hemangiomas, pyogenic granulomas, and kaposiform hemangioendothelioma, are characterized by abnormal cellular proliferation and demonstrate variable natural histories ranging from spontaneous involution to aggressive growth requiring intervention. In contrast, vascular malformations arise from embryologic errors in vasculogenesis and persist throughout life, progressively enlarging without regression. These include capillary, venous, lymphatic, and arteriovenous malformations, each with distinct clinical features and treatment considerations. Management is highly individualized and often necessi
key_findings: Comprehensive review of vascular anomalies distinguishing vascular tumours from malformations, including lymphatic malformations.
Vascular malformations, including lymphatic, are described as arising from embryologic errors in vasculogenesis, persisting lifelong and enlarging progressively without regression.
Management is described as individualised and multidisciplinary, spanning pharmacologic, sclerotherapy and surgical modalities.
papers.what_happened: A narrative review summarised the classification, complications and management of vascular anomalies, including developmental lymphatic malformations, oriented toward plastic and reconstructive surgery.
papers.why_it_matters: Lymphatic malformations sit alongside primary lymphedema in the developmental lymphatic disease spectrum, and classification errors between vascular tumours and malformations drive treatment mistakes.
papers.what_limits_confidence: Narrative review with no systematic search or evidence grading; it is educational synthesis rather than new data.

papers.title: Hand Surgery in Patients with a History of Lymphedema: A Review of Current Concepts and Opinions.
papers.abstract: Lymphedema may be primary (because of congenital lymphatic abnormalities) or secondary (commonly caused by cancer treatments). It progresses from pitting edema to fibrotic, nonpitting swelling. Diagnosis involves limb measurements and imaging like lymphoscintigraphy, indocyanine green lymphography, and magnetic resonance imaging lymphangiography. Treatment begins with complete decongestive therapy, and unresponsive cases may undergo microsurgical procedures such as lymphaticovenous shunts or vascularized lymph node transfer. Historically clinicians advised against procedures like needle sticks or tourniquet use in lymphedema-affected limbs. However, recent evidence disproves these concerns. Surveys show hand surgeons are more open to operating on lymphedema patients than other specialists. Several small studies report no considerable worsening of lymphedema after surgery, although transient flare-ups and minor infections have been noted. No studies confirmed deep infections, and most erythema-related cases resolved with oral antibiotics. Patients with prior breast cancer surgery, especially those who underwent axillary lymph node dissection, were previously thought to be at high risk. However, multiple studies show that hand surgery does not increase the risk of developing lymphedema in this group. Tourniquet use and avoiding routine prophylactic antibiotics are generally consi
key_findings: Review of current concepts on performing hand surgery in patients with lymphedema, explicitly distinguishing primary (congenital lymphatic abnormalities) from secondary disease.
Historical advice against needle sticks and tourniquet use in lymphedematous limbs is challenged by more recent evidence.
Surveys indicate hand surgeons are more willing than other specialists to operate on lymphedema-affected limbs.
Several small studies reported no considerable worsening of lymphedema after surgery, though transient flare-ups and minor infections occurred; no deep infections were confirmed.
papers.what_happened: A narrative review argued that longstanding precautions against venipuncture and tourniquet use in lymphedematous limbs are not supported by recent evidence, drawing on small studies and specialty surveys.
papers.why_it_matters: Blanket limb-precaution advice is a persistent source of restriction and anxiety for people with primary lymphedema, and relaxing it would change routine counselling if the underlying evidence held.
papers.what_limits_confidence: The supporting studies are small, uncontrolled and underpowered to detect uncommon harm, so absence of detected worsening is not evidence of safety; the review's language that recent evidence 'disproves' these concerns overstates what small observational series can establish.

papers.title: Cell-Free Adipose Liquid Extract Combined with Vascularized Lymph Node Transfer for Treating Lymphedema: Implications for Human Therapy.
papers.abstract: Rat hindlimb lymphedema model (popliteal lymph node excision) testing whether cell-free adipose liquid extract (ALE) enhances vascularized lymph node transfer (VLNT). Four arms: control, ALE only, VLNT only, VLNT+ALE. VLNT+ALE produced the fastest edema regression and more continuous lymphatic channels on ICG lymphography, with increased LYVE-1+ lymphangiogenesis and CD31+ angiogenesis on histology versus VLNT alone.
key_findings: In a rat surgical lymphedema model, adding cell-free adipose liquid extract to VLNT accelerated edema regression versus VLNT alone.
Combined treatment produced more continuous lymphatic channels on ICG lymphography and higher LYVE-1+ lymphatic vessel density on histology.
papers.what_happened: In a rat model of surgically induced lymphedema, adding a cell-free adipose liquid extract to vascularized lymph node transfer sped edema resolution and increased lymphangiogenesis markers versus VLNT alone.
papers.why_it_matters: VLNT is one of the few reconstructive options used in primary as well as secondary lymphedema, so an easily-sourced adjunct that improves lymphatic regrowth would be of interest if it translates to humans.
papers.what_limits_confidence: This is a small, short-follow-up rodent surgical-injury model (a secondary-lymphedema-type induction, not a genetic model) with only histologic and imaging surrogate endpoints, and lymphedema preclinical work has a poor record of translating to clinical benefit; the title's 'Implications for Human Therapy' is not supported by any human data.

papers.title: Cross-cultural validation and responsiveness of the French version of the lymphedema functioning, disability and health questionnaire for lower limb lymphedema (Lymph-ICF-LL).
papers.abstract: Observational study validating the French version of the Lymph-ICF-LL questionnaire (registered NCT07075549) for lower limb lymphedema. Patients with stable lower limb lymphedema completed the questionnaire twice 1-2 days apart to assess test-retest reliability (ICC), internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha), and construct validity (Spearman correlation with SF-36).
